Using the `coffee_data` example, suppose that the full model is: $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot X_1 + \beta_2 \cdot X_2 + \beta_3 \cdot X_3 + \epsilon$$ where $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, and $\beta_3$ are the parameters for the partial slopes of `aroma`, `flavor`, and `moisture_precentage`, respectively. The multiple linear regression outcomes using the `coffee_data` dataset on this model are stored in the object `mod_mult_1`. The reduced model does not contain the regressor `flavor` and is given by $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot X_1 + \beta_3 \cdot X_3 + \epsilon.$$ The multiple linear regression output using this model is stored in the object `mod_mult_2`. The hypothesis test for comparing the full and reduced models can be written as: $$\begin{aligned} H_0:\quad &Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot X_1 + \beta_2 \cdot X_2 + \epsilon\\ H_A:\quad &Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot X_1 + \beta_2 \cdot X_2 + \beta_3 \cdot X_3 + \epsilon \end{aligned}$$ or in words: $$\begin{aligned} H_0&:\quad \text{the reduced model is adequate}\\ H_A&:\quad \text{the full model is needed} \end{aligned}$$ This test is called an ANOVA test or an $F$-test, because the distribution of the test statistic follows an $F$ distribution. The way it works is that the test compares the sum of squared residuals of both the full and reduced models and determines whether the difference between these models was large enough to suggest that the full model is needed. To get the result of this test in R, we use the R function `anova()` and enter the reduced model followed by the full model with @tbl-mult-model-4 providing information for this test. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(mod_mult_2, mod_mult_1) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-mult-model-4 .cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

In particular, we continue using the plot of residuals against the fitted values and if no model violations are present the plot should be close to a null plot. While most of the treatment and interpretations are similar to those presented for simple linear regression, when the plot of residuals against fitted values is not a null plot, we know that there is some sort of violation to one or more of the assumptions of the model. It is no longer clear what is the reason for this, but at least one assumption is not met. On the other hand, if the residuals-against-fitted-values plot appears to be close to a null plot, none of the assumptions have been broken and we can proceed with the use of this model. Let's use the coffee example. Recall that we have shown that regressors `aroma`, `flavor`, and `continent_of_origin` were statistically significant, but `moisture_percentage` was not. So, we create a model only with the relevant regressors called `mod_mult_final`, determine the residuals, and create a plot of residuals against fitted values and a QQ-plot using the `grid.arrange()` function from the `gridExtra` package in @fig-grid-arrange-plot-check: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fit regression model: mod_mult_final <- lm(total_cup_points ~ aroma + flavor + continent_of_origin, coffee_data) # Get fitted values and residuals: fit_and_res_mult <- get_regression_points(mod_mult_final) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} g1 <- fit_and_res_mult |> ggplot(aes(x = total_cup_points_hat, y = residual)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "fitted values (total cup points)", y = "residual") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, col = "blue") g2 <- ggplot(fit_and_res_mult, aes(sample = residual)) + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line(col="blue", linewidth = 0.5) grid.arrange(g1, g2, ncol=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residuals vs. fitted values plot and QQ-plot for the multiple regression model.](10-inference-for-regression_files/figure-html/fig-grid-arrange-plot-check-1.png){#fig-grid-arrange-plot-check fig-align='center' fig-alt='Two diagnostic plots side by side: residuals-vs-fitted (left) and QQ-plot of residuals (right) for the multiple regression model.' width=\textwidth} ::: ::: The plot of residuals against fitted values (left) appears to be close to a null plot. This result is desirable because it supports the **L**inearity condition as no patterns are observed in this plot. The **E**qual or constant variance also holds as the vertical dispersion seems to be fairly uniform for any fitted values. Since we have assumed the data collected was random and there are no time sequences or other sequences to consider, the assumption of **I**ndependence seems to be acceptable too. Finally, the QQ-plot suggests (with the exception of one or two observations) that the residuals follow approximately the normal distribution. We can conclude that this model seems to be good enough to hold the assumptions of the model. This example concludes our treatment of theory-based inference. Whether the regression coefficients of one model are unbiased estimators. ::: ## Simulation-based Inference for multiple linear regression ### Confidence intervals for the partial slopes using `infer` We'll now use the simulation-based methods you previously learned in @sec-confidence-intervals and @sec-hypothesis-testing to compute ranges of plausible values for partial slopes with multiple linear regression. Each row is one predictor; horizontal segments are the CI bounds.' width=\textwidth} ::: ::: ### Hypothesis testing for the partial slopes using `infer` We can also conduct hypothesis tests for the partial slopes in multiple linear regression. We use the permutation test to test the null hypothesis $H_0: \beta_i = 0$ versus the alternative hypothesis $H_A: \beta_i \neq 0$ for each of the partial slopes. The `infer` package constructs the null distribution of the partial slopes under the null hypothesis of independence. #### Null distribution for the partial slopes {.unnumbered} We can also compute the null distribution for the partial slopes using the `infer` workflow. We will shuffle the values of the response variable `total_cup_points` across the values of the regressors `continent_of_origin`, `aroma`, `flavor`, and `moisture_percentage` in the `coffee_data` dataset. This is done under the assumption of independence between the response and the regressors. The syntax is similar to constructing the bootstrap distribution, but we use `type = "permute"` and set `hypothesize` to `null = "independence"`. We set our pseudo-random number generation seed to 2024 in order for the reader to get the same results with the shuffling. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2024) null_distribution_mlr <- coffee_quality |> specify(total_cup_points ~ continent_of_origin + aroma + flavor + moisture_percentage) |> hypothesize(null = "independence") |> generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |> fit() null_distribution_mlr ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7,000 × 3 # Groups: replicate [1,000] replicate term estimate 1 1 intercept 82.3 2 1 continent_of_originAsia -0.194 3 1 continent_of_originNorth America -0.371 4 1 continent_of_originSouth America -0.0830 5 1 aroma -1.22 6 1 flavor 1.52 7 1 moisture_percentage -0.0748 8 2 intercept 82.8 9 2 continent_of_originAsia -0.239 10 2 continent_of_originNorth America -0.617 # ℹ 6,990 more rows ``` ::: ::: #### Hypothesis tests for the partial slopes {.unnumbered} We can now conduct hypothesis tests for the partial slopes in multiple linear regression. We can use the permutation test to test the null hypothesis $H_0: \beta_i = 0$ versus the alternative hypothesis $H_A: \beta_i \neq 0$ for each of the partial slopes. Let's use a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$. We can visualize the $p$-values in the null distribution by comparing them to the observed test statistics. None of the above ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"} **(b)** A random "cloud" of points (no curvature, no funnel shape) supports linearity and equal variance. Normality is checked with a QQ-plot; independence is mostly a study-design question. ::: **Q3.** A theory-based *t*-test and a simulation-based permutation test for a regression slope often yield similar p-values when: a. The sample is very small b. The LINE conditions are met and the sample is reasonably large c. The model has many predictors d. The data is non-normal ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"} **(b)** When the assumptions hold and $n$ is reasonable, theory-based and simulation-based methods usually agree closely. They diverge most when assumptions fail — which is exactly when simulation-based methods earn their keep. ::: **Q4.** A regression model has slope = 0.5 and p-value = 0.001. The MOST precise conclusion: a. The slope is exactly 0.5 in the population b. **There is strong evidence that the population slope is not zero — but our estimate of the slope (0.5) still carries uncertainty (use a CI to quantify it)** c. The slope is significant at any $\alpha$ d. The relationship is causal ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"} **(b)** The point estimate is 0.5, but the population slope could plausibly be anywhere in the slope's CI. The p-value tests whether 0 is plausible, not whether 0.5 is correct. ::: **Q5.** A residual plot shows residuals fanning OUT (small at low fitted values, large at high fitted values). This violates which LINE condition? a. Linearity b. Independence c. **Equal variance** — the "E" in LINE d. Normality ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"} **(c)** Funnel-shaped residual spread = unequal variance. The "equal variance" assumption requires residuals to have roughly the SAME spread across the range of fitted values. When that fails, the SEs reported by `lm()` (which assume equal variance) are unreliable, and the resulting CIs/tests can be miscalibrated. The simulation-based workflow from §10.3 (bootstrap CIs, permutation tests via `infer`) doesn't lean on equal variance and is a good fallback. ::: **Q6.** A QQ-plot of residuals shows points sharply deviating from the diagonal at both tails. This suggests: a. Linearity is violated b. **The residuals are not Normal — at the extremes, observed residuals are more extreme than a Normal distribution would predict** c. Equal variance is violated d. Independence is violated ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"} **(b)** A QQ-plot lines up *observed quantiles* against *Normal quantiles*. When the tails of the cloud diverge from the diagonal, the actual residuals are more spread out at the extremes than a Normal distribution would predict — the "N" assumption is wobbly. Mild deviations are usually fine; extreme ones can make `lm()`'s theory-based CIs and $p$-values too aggressive (too narrow, too small) and the simulation-based workflow becomes the more honest choice. ::: **Q7.** When checking the *Independence* assumption, the most common diagnostic is: a. Histogram of $y$ ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"} **(c)** Independence is largely about *study design*: were the observations sampled independently, or do consecutive points share something (same person measured twice, same time period, same lab tech)? When the data has a natural ordering — by time, by sample number, by location — plotting residuals against that order can reveal repeating patterns or trends that suggest successive observations carry information about each other. If residuals look random with respect to order, the assumption is plausible. ::: **Q8.** A 95% CI for a slope is $(0.2, 0.8)$. A bug — they should be identical b. **Expected when LINE conditions are met and $n$ is reasonable; small differences come from finite simulation reps and minor approximations** c. Means LINE is violated d. Means the model is wrong ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show answer"} **(b)** When assumptions hold, the two approaches converge. Compare its width to the theory-based PI from EX 10.43. ```{webr-r} # Bootstrap prediction interval for a NEW observation: set.seed(76) new_height <- 200 boot_preds <- replicate(500, { s <- bball[sample(nrow(bball), nrow(bball), replace = TRUE), ] m <- lm(weight ~ height, data = s) pred_mean <- coef(m)[1] + coef(m)[2] * new_height # Add a residual draw to capture individual-level variation: pred_mean + sample(residuals(m), 1) }) quantile(boot_preds, c(0.025, 0.975)) ``` **EX10.47 (◆◆◆)** **Logistic regression with `glm()` (`moderndive`).** When the outcome is *binary* (yes/no, present/absent), linear regression is the wrong tool — predicted probabilities can fall outside $[0, 1]$. **Logistic regression**, fit with `glm(... family = "binomial")`, models the log-odds of the outcome and produces sensible probability predictions. The current `moderndive` package accepts `glm()` objects in all three `get_regression_*()` helpers, with `exponentiate = TRUE` giving you **odds ratios** instead of raw log-odds. Run the snippet. How does the interpretation of the slope change in this framework? ```{webr-r} # Build a binary outcome — "tall" (≥ 190 cm) yes/no: bball_log <- bball |> mutate(tall = ifelse(height >= 190, 1, 0)) # Logistic regression: model the LOG-ODDS of being "tall" as a linear function of weight m_logit <- glm(tall ~ weight, data = bball_log, family = "binomial") get_regression_table(m_logit) # Set exponentiate = TRUE for ODDS RATIOS instead of log-odds coefficients: get_regression_table(m_logit, exponentiate = TRUE) # get_regression_points returns fitted PROBABILITIES + residuals on the probability scale: get_regression_points(m_logit) |> head() ``` **EX10.48 (◆◆◆)** **AIC and BIC for model selection.** $R^2$ rewards complexity without penalty; **AIC** and **BIC** are alternative scores that *add* a penalty for each parameter. Both rules — "lower is better." BIC penalizes complexity more harshly than AIC (it tends to pick simpler models). Run the comparison on three nested `bball` models. Do AIC and BIC agree on which model wins? When would they disagree, and what would you do then? ```{webr-r} # AIC and BIC for model selection — lower is better. Both penalize complexity. m1 <- lm(weight ~ height, data = bball) m2 <- lm(weight ~ height + age, data = bball |> filter(!is.na(age))) m3 <- lm(weight ~ height + age + sex, data = bball |> filter(!is.na(age))) AIC(m1, m2, m3) BIC(m1, m2, m3) ``` **EX10.49 (◆◆◆)** **Simpson's paradox in real data.** When you collapse across groups, the *pooled* slope can have the opposite sign (or a very different magnitude) than the *within-group* slope. The pattern is famous because it's *not* a math trick — it's the same data, summarized differently, telling different stories. Run the snippet on Gymnastics + Basketball. Briefly — which is the "true" story, and how would you decide *when* to report the pooled vs the per-group slope? ```{webr-r} # Construct a Simpson's paradox setup using bball: # Across all sports, taller athletes might weigh LESS per cm (slope < 1) # But within each sport, the per-cm slope is steeper (slope > 1) set.seed(76) library(olympicAthletes) sub <- olympic_athletes |> filter(sport %in% c("Gymnastics", "Basketball"), !is.na(height), !is.na(weight)) pooled <- coef(lm(weight ~ height, data = sub))[2] per_sport <- sub |> group_by(sport) |> summarize(slope = coef(lm(weight ~ height))[2], .groups = "drop") list(pooled_slope = pooled, per_sport = per_sport) ``` **EX10.50 (◆◆◆)** **Inference with in-formula transforms (`moderndive`).** Earlier, transforming the outcome (`log(weight)`) inside `lm()` could leak ugly column names like `` `log(weight)` `` into the `get_regression_points()` output. The current `moderndive` package handles this — the LHS transform is sanitized to a clean name like `log_weight`/`log_weight_hat`, and the `get_regression_table()` slope still has a valid CI you can interpret. Run the snippet. In one sentence, what does a slope of, say, 0.012 *mean* on a `log(weight)`-vs-height regression? (Hint — convert via $e^{0.012} \approx 1.012$ → about a 1.2 % change per cm.) ```{webr-r} # In-formula transforms now work cleanly with moderndive's get_regression_* helpers m_log <- lm(log(weight) ~ height, data = bball) get_regression_table(m_log) # slope interprets as % change in weight per cm get_regression_points(m_log) |> # outcome column is sanitized to log_weight head() ``` **EX10.51 (◆◆◆)** **Robust regression with `MASS::rlm()`.** When LINE diagnostics flag heavy tails or outliers (Ch 10 § 10.2.6), you have two options — (1) trust the bootstrap inference machinery, or (2) switch to an **estimator that's less sensitive to extreme values**. **`MASS::rlm()`** (robust linear model) iteratively down-weights observations with large residuals. Run both fits and compare slopes. When would you prefer `rlm()` over OLS — and what do you give up in exchange? ```{webr-r} # rlm() fits a robust regression (down-weights influential outliers). # We use the qualified MASS::rlm() instead of library(MASS) — attaching # MASS would mask dplyr::select() in your downstream code. m_ols <- lm(weight ~ height, data = bball) m_rlm <- MASS::rlm(weight ~ height, data = bball) list(ols_slope = coef(m_ols)["height"], rlm_slope = coef(m_rlm)["height"]) ``` **EX10.52 (◆◆◆)** **Bootstrap CI for a partial slope (extension of EX 10.18).** The chapter's bootstrap workflow handled *simple*-LR slopes via `infer`. For a *partial* slope (one slope inside a multi-predictor model), you can roll your own — resample rows of `pl2`, refit `m_par` on each, pull the `radius_earth` coefficient, and percentile the resulting distribution. Compare your bootstrap CI to the theory-based CI from EX 10.13's regression table. When are they close? When might they diverge? ```{webr-r} set.seed(76) # Bootstrap a partial slope under a parallel-slopes model on planets: # (reuse pl2 from EX 10.13) boot_slopes <- replicate(500, { idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(pl2)), nrow(pl2), replace = TRUE) coef(lm(mass_earth ~ radius_earth + discovery_method, data = pl2[idx, ]))["radius_earth"] }) quantile(boot_slopes, c(0.025, 0.975)) ``` **EX10.53 (◆◆◆)** **Confidence bands on a regression plot.** `geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE)` (the default) adds a shaded *confidence band* around each fitted line. The band is a visual summary of how precisely the *mean* response is estimated at each value of $x$ — wider where data is sparse or scatter is large, narrower where data is dense and tightly clustered. Earlier figures in this chapter used `se = FALSE` to keep the lines clean; here, turn the bands back on for the `pl2` parallel-slopes setup. Which discovery method's slope has the wider band, and why does that make sense given the data? ```{webr-r} library(ggplot2) # pl2 = top-2-discovery-method subset of planets (see EX 10.13) planets_lite <- planets |> filter(!is.na(mass_earth), !is.na(radius_earth), !is.na(discovery_method)) top2 <- planets_lite |> count(discovery_method, sort = TRUE) |> head(2) |> pull(discovery_method) pl2 <- planets_lite |> filter(discovery_method %in% top2) ggplot(pl2, aes(x = radius_earth, y = mass_earth, color = discovery_method)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) + labs(title = "Parallel-slopes fit with 95% confidence bands") ``` **EX10.54 (◆◆◆)** **$R^2$, adjusted $R^2$, and the F-statistic — three whole-model summary numbers.** Beyond the per-coefficient regression table, `summary(lm(...))` reports three numbers that describe the model as a whole: * $R^2$ — the fraction of variance in $y$ that the fitted model explains. Adding any predictor (useful or not) can only *raise* $R^2$. * Adjusted $R^2$ — same idea, but penalized for the number of predictors. Adding a *useless* predictor will typically *lower* this (EX 55 demonstrates). * F-statistic — the omnibus test that *at least one* slope is non-zero ($H_0$: all slopes simultaneously zero). Fit `lm(weight ~ height + sex, data = bball)` and pull all three. What does the F-test's $p$-value tell you that the per-coefficient $p$-values don't? ```{webr-r} bball <- olympic_athletes |> filter(sport == "Basketball", !is.na(height), !is.na(weight), !is.na(sex)) m <- lm(weight ~ height + sex, data = bball) s <- summary(m) c(R2 = s$r.squared, adj_R2 = s$adj.r.squared, F_stat = unname(s$fstatistic["value"]), F_p_value = pf(s$fstatistic["value"], s$fstatistic["numdf"], s$fstatistic["dendf"], lower.tail = FALSE)) ``` **EX10.55 (◆◆◆)** **Adjusted $R^2$ penalizes a useless predictor (pairs with EX 54).** Add a column of pure noise (`rnorm()`) to `bball` — completely unrelated to anything — then refit the weight model both with and without this noise predictor. Compare each pair of $R^2$ values: the *unadjusted* $R^2$ will at best be flat or rise a hair (more predictors always explain at least as much variance in the *training* data), but the *adjusted* version will typically drop. Why does the adjustment go *down* for a useless predictor, and what does this say about using raw $R^2$ alone to compare models? ```{webr-r} bball <- olympic_athletes |> filter(sport == "Basketball", !is.na(height), !is.na(weight), !is.na(sex)) set.seed(123) bball_aug <- bball |> mutate(noise = rnorm(n())) # With useless predictor: c(R2_with = summary(lm(weight ~ height + sex + noise, data = bball_aug))$r.squared, adjR2_with = summary(lm(weight ~ height + sex + noise, data = bball_aug))$adj.r.squared) # Without: c(R2_without = summary(lm(weight ~ height + sex, data = bball_aug))$r.squared, adjR2_without = summary(lm(weight ~ height + sex, data = bball_aug))$adj.r.squared) ``` **EX10.56 (◆◆◆)** **Simulation-based CI for each partial slope (`infer::fit()`).** Section 10.6 walks through a four-step `infer` pipeline on the coffee data — `specify()` → `generate(type = "bootstrap")` → `fit()`, then `get_confidence_interval()` with the observed `fit()` as the point estimate. Apply the same pipeline to the exoplanet parallel-slopes model `mass_earth ~ radius_earth + discovery_method` on `pl2`. Read the bootstrap percentile CI for the `radius_earth` partial slope. Does it exclude 0? How does it compare to the *theory-based* CI you pulled from `get_regression_table(m_par)` in EX 10.21? ```{webr-r} planets_lite <- planets |> filter(!is.na(radius_earth), !is.na(mass_earth), !is.na(discovery_method)) top2 <- planets_lite |> count(discovery_method, sort = TRUE) |> head(2) |> pull(discovery_method) pl2 <- planets_lite |> filter(discovery_method %in% top2) set.seed(76) observed_fit <- pl2 |> specify(mass_earth ~ radius_earth + discovery_method) |> fit() boot_distn <- pl2 |> specify(mass_earth ~ radius_earth + discovery_method) |> generate(reps = 500, type = "bootstrap") |> fit() boot_distn |> get_confidence_interval( level = 0.95, type = "percentile", point_estimate = observed_fit ) ``` **EX10.57 (◆◆◆)** **Permutation $p$-value for each partial slope.** Section 10.6 also shows the *null-distribution* counterpart to the bootstrap CI — swap `type = "bootstrap"` for `hypothesize(null = "independence") |> generate(reps = ..., type = "permute") |> fit()`, then call `get_p_value()` with `obs_stat = observed_fit`. Run this pipeline for `pl2`. Report the $p$-value for `radius_earth` and for the `discovery_method` offset. Where does each observed slope land relative to its null distribution in the `shade_p_value()` plot, and what does that visual placement tell you about the strength of evidence for each predictor? ```{webr-r} planets_lite <- planets |> filter(!is.na(radius_earth), !is.na(mass_earth), !is.na(discovery_method)) top2 <- planets_lite |> count(discovery_method, sort = TRUE) |> head(2) |> pull(discovery_method) pl2 <- planets_lite |> filter(discovery_method %in% top2) set.seed(2024) observed_fit <- pl2 |> specify(mass_earth ~ radius_earth + discovery_method) |> fit() null_distn <- pl2 |> specify(mass_earth ~ radius_earth + discovery_method) |> hypothesize(null = "independence") |> generate(reps = 500, type = "permute") |> fit() null_distn |> get_p_value(obs_stat = observed_fit, direction = "two-sided") visualize(null_distn) + shade_p_value(obs_stat = observed_fit, direction = "two-sided") ``` **EX10.58 (◆◆◆)** **When theory-based and simulation-based agree (and disagree).** For the `pl2` model from EX 10.56–10.57, the theory-based regression table from `get_regression_table(m_par)` and the `infer` bootstrap CI both report a 95 % CI for the `radius_earth` partial slope. In Chapter 10 they agreed closely.
